topic: Machine Learning: Classification vs Regression Scenarios

questions.scenario: A high-frequency IoT telemetry system in an industrial manufacturing plant monitors CNC spindle health via vibration, acoustic, and thermal sensors at 1 kHz. The business requirement is to prevent catastrophic failure by issuing maintenance alerts. The target failure event occurs in fewer than 0.08% of operational hours. The initial modeling team formulated the problem as a continuous regression task predicting Remaining Useful Life (RUL) in hours using an LSTM network. However, the model exhibits severe error in production: spindle run-to-failure records are heavily right-censored, early degradation cycles are noisy and indistinguishable from normal operation, and the model struggles to meet a hard 5ms edge-inference latency constraint.
questions.question: To resolve the label censoring issues, severe target skewness, and edge-latency limitations while guaranteeing an actionable maintenance intervention window of 4 hours, which pipeline redesign is mathematically and architecturally most appropriate?
options: A) Retain continuous RUL regression, transform the target using Box-Cox transformation to reduce skew, and replace the LSTM with an ElasticNet regression model to satisfy the 5ms latency constraint.

B) Reformulate into a time-windowed binary classification task predicting whether spindle failure will occur within the next 4 hours ($T_{event} \le 4$), train a Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (GBDT) on rolling-window summary statistics, and optimize with Focal Loss or asymmetric cost matrices.

C) Treat degradation as a multi-class ordinal classification problem (Normal, Minor Wear, Critical Wear, Failure) and train an ensemble of Support Vector Machines (SVM) with a Gaussian radial basis kernel.
D) Retain the regression formulation but optimize directly via Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) loss to penalize percentage errors equally across both early and late degradation phases.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Reformulate into a time-windowed binary classification task predicting whether spindle failure will occur within the next 4 hours ($T_{event} \le 4$), train a Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (GBDT) on rolling-window summary statistics, and optimize with Focal Loss or asymmetric cost matrices.
questions.explanation: When predicting Remaining Useful Life (RUL) under high sensor noise, severe right-censoring, and heavy class imbalance (<0.08% failures), continuous regression models struggle because exact continuous time-to-failure labels for healthy components are unknown (censored) and early degradation is non-linear. Reformulating the objective into a fixed-horizon binary classification problem ('Will failure occur in [t, t + 4h]?') directly aligns with maintenance operations. Using GBDTs over pre-aggregated rolling features reduces sequence model compute overhead, easily meeting the 5ms edge latency constraint, while Focal Loss or cost-sensitive reweighting mitigates the extreme class imbalance.

questions.scenario: A financial risk platform processes loan loss forecasting on short-term merchant credit advances over 15,000 sparse categorical features (e.g., MCC codes, cross-border tags, transaction graphs). Analysis reveals that 95.5% of merchants never default, producing an exact observed dollar loss of $0.00. For the 4.5% that do default, the actual loss distribution is strictly positive, highly dispersed, and heavy-tailed (Pareto-distributed) up to $2,000,000. Fitting a single global Ridge or LightGBM regressor with Mean Squared Error (MSE) on the entire dataset leads to pervasive under-prediction of large defaults and non-zero predictions for zero-loss merchants.
questions.question: Which modeling strategy is theoretically best suited to handle this zero-inflated, semicontinuous target distribution across a high-dimensional feature space?
options: A) A single deep Feed-Forward Neural Network trained with a Huber loss function after applying a log1p transformation to both input features and the loss target.

B) A two-stage hurdle framework: first train an L1-regularized binary classifier (or GBDT) to predict the probability of default ($Loss > 0$), and conditionally train a generalized linear model or GBDT regressor with a Tweedie or log-link Gamma deviance objective on the defaulting cohort.

C) Discretize the continuous dollar loss into 10 uniform dollar ranges, treat the problem as an unweighted multi-class classification problem, and compute expected loss as the dot product of bin centroids and Softmax probabilities.
D) Apply unsupervised k-Means clustering to partition the feature space into homogeneous risk buckets, followed by standard Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression within each cluster.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) A two-stage hurdle framework: first train an L1-regularized binary classifier (or GBDT) to predict the probability of default ($Loss > 0$), and conditionally train a generalized linear model or GBDT regressor with a Tweedie or log-link Gamma deviance objective on the defaulting cohort.
questions.explanation: The target variable is semicontinuous and zero-inflated: it has a discrete probability mass at zero ($Y=0$) and a skewed, heavy-tailed continuous distribution for positive values ($Y>0$). Standard regression with MSE assumes additive Gaussian errors, which breaks down entirely under zero-inflation. A Hurdle/Two-Stage model isolates the two processes: Stage 1 evaluates the classification boundary ($P(Y > 0|X)$), and Stage 2 evaluates the continuous conditional expectation ($E[Y | Y > 0, X]$) using a distribution suited for strictly positive, skewed loss figures (such as a Gamma or Tweedie deviance). This avoids zero-contamination in the regression stage and eliminates artificial non-zero predictions for non-defaulters.

questions.scenario: An enterprise e-commerce platform surfaces personalized product recommendations on its home feed. The catalog contains 5 million active SKUs. The engineering team deployed a continuous regression model trained to predict each user's purchase probability ($p \in [0, 1]$) using Mean Squared Error (MSE) on offline historical logs. While offline evaluation showed an outstandingly low Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE = 0.012), live AB testing showed a 9% decline in gross revenue and a steep drop in Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG@10) compared to an older binary classifier trained using pairwise logistic ranking loss.
questions.question: What is the primary mathematical reason that minimizing continuous regression error (RMSE) failed to optimize the top-k recommendation performance compared to the ranking-oriented classification approach?
options: A) RMSE applies uniform quadratic penalties across the entire target space, allowing millions of non-purchased tail items ($p \approx 0$) to dominate the gradient and compromise the relative ordering of high-probability candidate items at the top of the slate.

B) Continuous regression models intrinsically suffer from the curse of dimensionality when processing high-cardinality item IDs, while classification models automatically compress feature spaces through log-odds mapping.
C) The binary cross-entropy loss function is mathematically non-convex when applied to click-through data, whereas MSE guarantees convergence to the global Pareto-optimal ranking permutation.
D) Logistic regression with ranking loss inherently corrects for covariate shift, whereas regression with MSE produces uncalibrated probabilities that invalidate post-processing temperature scaling.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) RMSE applies uniform quadratic penalties across the entire target space, allowing millions of non-purchased tail items ($p \approx 0$) to dominate the gradient and compromise the relative ordering of high-probability candidate items at the top of the slate.
questions.explanation: Pointwise regression via RMSE treats every item pair equally across the entire dataset. In recommendations, over 99% of items are irrelevant ($y=0$). Minimizing RMSE causes the optimization algorithm to focus heavily on driving errors close to zero for the massive majority of unpurchased items, at the expense of correct pairwise ordering among the small subset of relevant items. However, business metrics (NDCG@10, Revenue) depend strictly on the relative ranking order of top-k items. Pairwise ranking and classification losses explicitly penalize inverted ranks between positive and negative candidates, aligning loss optimization directly with top-k ranking quality.
